description: We are passionate aerospace engineering students willing to gain knowledge in space studies by joining space related STEM competions.
summary:
We created a aerospace-grade interactive web console to synthesize NASA's combustion data, such as Saffire, BASS-II and FLEX, into a single source.

Our dashboard provides engineering insights from isolated microgravity fire data to help solve the "Flame in Freefall" challenge. It incorporates an interactive Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) ranking engine, a live Flammability Risk Simulator and a Cross-Experiment Matrix. Users can dynamically visualize flame morphology for different gravity environments (Lunar, Martian, Microgravity), change cabin parameters such as cabin oxygen concentration and ventilation, and directly compare materials to NASA-STD-6001B safety limits.

This solution is essential since fire's behavior is fundamentally different off Earth, e.g., cool flames that are invisible and change the limits of flammability of materials in different airflow conditions. Humanity is developing lunar habitats and spacecraft for deep space travel, and this is a tool to connect the dots between raw experimental data and implementation. It allows mission planners and aerospace engineers to rapidly compare decades of research, optimize spacecraft cabin atmospheres and design effective and life saving firefighting solutions for future exploration.
details:
FireWise console is a deterministic, aerospace, interactive web dashboard that combines decades of microgravity combustion data from the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database. The application processes complex experimental data from missions such as Saffire I-VI, BASS-II and FLEX to convert raw data into actionable, visual telemetry. It has at its heart a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) tool that can be used to compute material flammability and hazard scores using user inputted weights. This is coupled with a Flammability Risk Simulator that displays real-time flame morphological changes as a function of different cabin conditions, and a Cross-Experiment Matrix that compares specific materials to the NASA-STD-6001B safety threshold.

The project will reduce the number of spreadsheets NASA engineers will need to cross reference and research papers to look at, by combining the various combustion campaigns in one place. This merger directly boosts and protects human deep space exploration. Flame behavior changes significantly when the environment changes from microgravity on the International Space Station to 0.16g on the Moon and 0.38g on Mars. The dashboard provides the exact information ECLSS engineers require to fine-tune the cabin atmosphere, choose safe materials and develop efficient fire suppression plans for different gravity levels.

Architecture is written in React (JSX) with dynamic state management in JavaScript, styled with Tailwind CSS and packaged as a standalone web application for easy embedding on platforms such as Google Sites. The simulations of combustion ducts are performed live using native manipulation of the SVG. The interface is a true “NASA Glenn Research Center telemetry workstation” and not a standard corporate look or AI generated by a generative tool that might hallucinate important safety information. It uses a 100% deterministic, mathematically transparent model in which the user may physically move the sliders, and see the effect they have on the outputs of safety parameters such as Damköhler and Péclet numbers.

The team has always strived to balance the scientific rigor with the ease of use, not only during development, but also in ensuring the strict aerodynamic and thermodynamic accuracy without stirring confusion among non-specialist project managers. Future teams can easily add custom experiment rows and modify their ranking algorithms, understanding that NASA continually carries out new experiments, the architecture provides a built-in Live Editor and an Export Studio. The tool is particularly flexible and applicable because it explicitly considers variable gravity limits and suppression metrics needed, directly addressing the unique challenges of the environment for the Artemis generation and beyond.
